strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically useful limitation of controllable video generation: specifying pitch and roll relative to gravity without requiring an initial reference frame. Using calibrated panoramic videos to obtain broad orientation coverage is intuitive and well motivated.

The null-pitch captioning strategy identifies a genuine conflict between textual semantics and camera conditioning. Its ablation reports meaningful improvements in pitch, gravity, and relative-rotation errors, and Fig. 6 provides a clear qualitative illustration.
The method substantially improves the reported camera-control metrics over AC3D and the PreciseCam-plus-WAN pipeline, while using a lightweight ControlNet-style adaptation of an established backbone.

The presentation is generally clear, with an effective pipeline diagram, useful distribution analysis, qualitative comparisons, and an explicit limitations section acknowledging rotational-only augmentation and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The experimental design does not isolate the central contribution. The proposed model differs from AC3D in training data, orientation distribution, captioning, and pose representation. The alleged absolute-Plücker baseline merely feeds absolute poses to a pretrained model for which they are out of distribution. A decisive comparison would retrain the same architecture on the same WEB360 crops and captions using relative versus gravity-aligned conditioning, alongside separate ablations of panoramic sampling and null-pitch captions.

The evaluation benchmark is small (140 videos), and FID/FVD are especially questionable at this sample size. No confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or significance analysis are reported. The differing numbers for the full method in Tables 1 and 2 are also unexplained.

Camera accuracy is measured through Perspective Fields and VGGT predictions rather than direct ground-truth observations, but the paper does not validate these estimators on generated videos or extreme and pole-adjacent viewpoints. Estimator failure can be correlated with generation quality and viewpoint, potentially confounding the reported gains.

The mathematical camera specification is insufficiently precise and appears inconsistent. With t described as the camera origin and E=[R|t] behaving as a camera-to-world pose, a ray direction should be proportional to R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T; adding t before normalization, as written in Sec. 3.1, does not produce a translation-invariant ray direction. Equation 2 and the definition of phi are likewise deferred without enough convention details to verify the claimed gravity alignment.

The claim of 'absolute camera control' is overstated: the paper explicitly leaves yaw unconstrained, translation is not globally grounded across scenes, and the sampling augmentation supports only rotations. The demonstrated capability is more accurately absolute gravity-referenced pitch and roll control.

The quality trade-off is material rather than negligible: the method has the lowest CLIP score and worse FID than every listed baseline, while its FVD is worse than the PreciseCam-plus-WAN baseline. More human evaluation and temporal-quality analysis are needed to establish that improved estimated pose accuracy yields better usable videos.

Reproducibility is limited by important details being deferred to supplementary material, including the complete gravity transform, trajectory construction for evaluation, and WAN results. The benchmark is promised only upon publication, and the main paper gives no code or checkpoint release commitment.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and underexplored problem: controlling video-camera pitch and roll relative to gravity, rather than only specifying motion relative to the first frame.
The use of calibrated panoramic videos to synthesize diverse viewpoints is intuitive and potentially valuable, especially for rare top-down, low-angle, and Dutch-angle shots.
Null-pitch captioning is a simple, practically motivated response to conflicts between textual content and camera orientation. The reported ablation shows improvements across all listed metrics.
The paper is generally well organized, and the qualitative examples help communicate the intended capability. Reported camera errors improve substantially over the selected baselines.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence does not isolate the central contribution. The method is trained on panoramic data specifically constructed to cover extreme orientations, whereas AC3D uses its released RealEstate10K-trained checkpoint. There is no controlled comparison in which relative and absolute representations are trained on the same data, architecture, schedule, and captions. Feeding absolute Plucker rays to a model for which they are out of distribution is not a meaningful representation ablation.

The proposed benchmark is too weak to substantiate the broad claims. It contains only 140 manually filtered videos, roll is introduced through image warping, and evaluation trajectories replace the source rotations with newly sampled ones. Consequently, the reference videos do not depict the requested target views, making the interpretation of FID/FVD unclear and preventing reference-based validation of the generated geometry.

Absolute orientation accuracy is measured using Perspective Fields on generated frames, but the paper does not validate this estimator on generated content or extreme/polar viewpoints—the precise regime under study. The same estimator is also involved in benchmark construction. No human evaluation, synthetic calibration experiment, or uncertainty analysis supports the metric's reliability.

The mathematical presentation of Plucker rays appears incorrect or at least conventionally inconsistent: the stated ray direction includes translation, d = R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T + t, although translation should affect the ray origin rather than its direction under a camera-to-world convention. The extrinsic convention and transformation composition in Eq. (2) are insufficiently specified, impairing technical confidence and reproducibility.

The method does not provide fully absolute camera control as repeatedly claimed. Pitch and roll are gravity-referenced, but yaw is explicitly unconstrained; translation is inherited only relatively and the sampling procedure supports rotational motion alone. The novelty and claims should therefore be framed more narrowly as gravity-referenced tilt control.

The baseline set is not sufficiently diagnostic: the PreciseCam-plus-WAN cascade changes models and generation protocol, textual pose prompting is a weak substitute for retraining, and no same-data relative-pose baseline, gravity-alignment ablation, sampling-distribution ablation, or alternative captioning strategy is provided. Only the null-pitch component receives a quantitative ablation.

Results are reported for a single training run without confidence intervals or significance analysis. Moreover, the nominally complete method has unexplained differences between Tables 1 and 2 (for example, pitch error 23.79 versus 23.11 and FVD 896.84 versus 937.62), which raises questions about evaluation consistency.

Important reproducibility details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material, including trajectory generation for evaluation and essential training settings. Dataset attribution is also inconsistent: WEB360 is associated with citation [15] in one place and [34] elsewhere, while those entries correspond to ViPE and 360DVD, respectively.

The method sacrifices semantic and perceptual metrics relative to several baselines, and visible generation artifacts remain. Given the unfairly controlled comparisons and uncertain evaluation metrics, the current manuscript does not establish that the gains arise from the proposed absolute representation rather than the specialized training distribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored limitation of camera-controlled video generation: existing relative-pose conditioning cannot directly specify orientation with respect to gravity. The gravity-aligned formulation provides intuitive control over absolute pitch and roll without requiring an initial reference frame.

The use of calibrated 360-degree videos is a clever and scalable way to overcome the strong forward-facing bias of conventional video datasets. Sampling perspective crops across the sphere exposes the model to top-down, low-angle, and Dutch-angle views that are otherwise rare.

Null-pitch conditioning is well motivated: captions from rotated crops can entangle scene content with viewpoint and compete with camera conditioning. The ablation supports its value, reducing pitch error from 28.75 to 23.11, gravity error from 31.70 to 26.20, and relative rotation error from 21.55 to 15.79.

The principal quantitative results are encouraging. Relative to AC3D, the proposed method substantially improves absolute pitch error (41.65 to 23.79), gravity error (46.30 to 27.06), and relative rotation error (27.81 to 14.25). The qualitative results also show meaningful improvements at unusual orientations.

The method reuses a lightweight ControlNet-style architecture with a CogVideoX-2B backbone, suggesting that the main ideas concern data and geometric conditioning rather than requiring a costly new generator. The paper is generally clear, visually effective, and candid about limitations involving translation and generation artifacts.
The proposed SpatialVID-extreme benchmark targets a genuine evaluation gap by deliberately covering extreme pitch and roll, where existing camera-control benchmarks provide little evidence.
weaknesses: The central comparison is substantially confounded by training data and captioning. The proposed model is trained on augmented WEB360 data with null-pitch captions, whereas the main AC3D checkpoint was trained on RealEstate10K. A controlled baseline trained with the same WEB360 crops, captions, backbone, optimization, and compute—but using relative poses—is needed to isolate the benefit of absolute gravity-aligned conditioning.

The AC3D plus absolute Plücker baseline feeds absolute poses to a pretrained model that was not trained for them, so its poor performance is expected and does not constitute a strong test of the representation. The PreciseCam-plus-WAN baseline is also a heterogeneous two-stage system. Consequently, the paper lacks a closely matched competing baseline.

The evaluation benchmark contains only 140 videos. FID and especially FVD are unreliable at this scale, and no confidence intervals, repeated trials, or statistical uncertainty are reported. The absolute-pose metrics also depend on Perspective Fields estimates for generated frames, but the accuracy and failure rate of this estimator under the very extreme views being evaluated are not validated.

The ablation study isolates only null-pitch conditioning. It does not separately measure the effects of gravity alignment, absolute versus relative Plücker rays under matched training, spherical trajectory augmentation, the amount of 360-degree training data, or the stated 50% null-pitch mixture. These omissions make it difficult to determine which components account for the main gains.

There are unexplained numerical inconsistencies between the main and ablation tables: the reported full-model results differ across them, including pitch error (23.79 versus 23.11) and FVD (896.84 versus 937.62). The manuscript should state whether these use different splits, seeds, checkpoints, or evaluation settings.

The scope of “absolute camera control” is narrower than the phrasing sometimes suggests. Gravity resolves pitch and roll, but yaw remains unconstrained, translation is inherited from SfM in an arbitrary-scale frame, and the sampling augmentation supports only rotational motion. The paper eventually explains some of this, but the claims should consistently say gravity-referenced absolute orientation rather than fully absolute camera pose.

The camera-ray definition appears technically ambiguous: the manuscript computes the purported ray direction as R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T plus t before normalization. Under the usual camera-to-world convention, translation determines the ray origin and should not be added to its direction. The pose convention and actual implementation need clarification. Algorithm 1 is similarly unclear about whether the initial sampled rotation is included or overwritten.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main paper, including exact data filtering, benchmark prompts and trajectory generation, optimization hyperparameters, and evaluation preprocessing. Attribution is also inconsistent: WEB360 is associated with different citations in different sections. The promised release helps, but the benchmark construction includes manual filtering whose criteria should be documented.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is explicitly declared. The paper addresses an important and underexplored limitation of camera-controlled video generation: precise control at extreme pitch and roll angles in a gravity-aligned frame.

The use of 360-degree videos to synthesize broad orientation coverage is intuitive and practically valuable. The pipeline combines panorama projection, estimated gravity, camera motion, randomized rotations, and field-of-view variation into a coherent training procedure.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, insightful response to prompt-camera entanglement. The ablation is substantial: removing it increases PitchErr from 9.35 to 15.78 degrees and GravityErr from 11.67 to 17.72 degrees.

The method clearly improves the principal target metrics over the closest gravity-aware baseline, UCPE: PitchErr improves from 16.25 to 9.35 degrees, GravityErr from 18.88 to 11.67 degrees, and RotErr from 18.38 to 15.96 degrees. Qualitative results also support better handling of extreme views.
The proposed SpatialVID-extreme benchmark and the separate 380-pair prompt-camera entanglement test expose failure modes poorly represented in conventional forward-facing video benchmarks.

The paper is well organized and visually clear, provides relevant comparisons, reports computational requirements, and candidly acknowledges limitations involving translation augmentation and generation artifacts.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly isolate the source of the improvement. The compared systems use different backbones and capacities—e.g., the proposed method uses WAN-2.2 5B, whereas AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B and UCPE uses WAN-2.1—and there is no same-backbone comparison trained on the same panoramic data with relative versus gravity-aligned conditioning. The AC3D absolute-Plücker variant is especially difficult to interpret if absolute poses are merely substituted into a model trained for relative poses.

Ablations are too limited for a multi-component pipeline. Beyond null-pitch conditioning, the paper does not isolate panoramic trajectory augmentation, gravity alignment, the pole-biased sampling distribution, field-of-view augmentation, or the added look-down caption/negative-prompt procedure.

Evaluation partly depends on the same Perspective Fields estimator used to create gravity annotations. PitchErr and GravityErr may therefore inherit estimator bias, particularly at extreme orientations, yet no independent human, sensor-based, or synthetic calibration validates these measurements.

SpatialVID-extreme contains only 140 videos. FID and especially FVD are unstable at this scale, but the paper gives no confidence intervals, repeated-generation statistics, or significance analysis. The reported quality tradeoff is also nontrivial: the full method has worse CLIP, FID, FVD, and TransErr than its no-null-pitch ablation.

The benchmark mixes real reference videos with newly sampled rotation trajectories rather than paired ground-truth videos rendered along those trajectories. This is suitable for testing estimated pose adherence, but it weakens the interpretation of FID/FVD and prevents direct assessment of scene fidelity under the requested camera path.

The prompt-camera entanglement benchmark uses only 20 panoramas, and Figure 6 shifts each method's CLIP scores by its own mean. That visualization highlights variation but obscures absolute semantic quality, so the claim of maximizing content similarity is not fully established.

The term “absolute camera control” is broader than the implemented reference frame: pitch and roll are gravity grounded, but yaw remains arbitrary and translations come from the source videos rather than being freely augmented. The paper explains these qualifications, but several headline claims such as “arbitrary” control overstate the demonstrated capability.

Reproducibility commitments are incomplete in the manuscript: the benchmarks are promised for release, but an equally clear commitment for code, trained checkpoints, processed training annotations, and filtering details is absent. Potential overlap between the YouTube-derived PanoVid training set and SpatialVID evaluation sources is also not analyzed.

strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of camera-controlled video generation: specifying pitch and roll relative to gravity, especially at extreme orientations. Training from perspective crops of panoramic videos is a sensible way to obtain broader orientation coverage than ordinary videos provide.

The null-pitch captioning idea identifies a real prompt–camera conflict and is supported by a useful ablation: removing it increases pitch error from 9.35° to 15.78° and gravity error from 11.67° to 17.72° on the proposed benchmark.
The method substantially improves the reported orientation metrics over the dynamic-video baselines, and the qualitative examples suggest better handling of upward, downward, and looping rotations.

The manuscript is generally well organized, illustrates the data pipeline clearly, compares against several relevant recent systems, and acknowledges limitations concerning translation sampling and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not sufficiently independent. Perspective Fields is used to derive gravity information for training, select benchmark videos by pitch, and estimate pitch and gravity in generated outputs. This circularity may reward reproduction of the estimator's biases rather than genuine geometric compliance. There is no independent calibration, synthetic test with known geometry, or human evaluation to validate the main conclusion.

The baseline comparison is heavily confounded. The proposed method uses WAN-2.2 5B, whereas UCPE uses WAN-2.1 and AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B. There is no controlled comparison using the same backbone, training data, compute, and camera encoder. Moreover, feeding absolute Plücker coordinates to an AC3D checkpoint trained for relative coordinates creates an out-of-distribution input and is not a valid ablation of absolute versus relative conditioning.

The paper does not isolate several claimed contributions. It ablates null-pitch conditioning but not gravity alignment, panoramic trajectory sampling, pose filtering, or the absolute representation. Consequently, the reported gains cannot be attributed clearly to the proposed components rather than the different backbone and training corpus.

Claims of absolute and precise camera control are overstated. The formulation fixes only gravity-referenced pitch and roll; yaw remains unconstrained, position retains an arbitrary origin, and metric translation is not demonstrated. Translation error is computed only after scale normalization, the method has the worst reported dynamic-model TransErr (0.72), and training cannot synthesize new translations. Thus the illustrated command to move forward by eight meters is unsupported by the evaluation.

The camera representation is technically unclear and possibly incorrect as written. Section 3.1 defines a ray direction as R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T+t even though t is also called the camera origin; a direction from that origin should subtract t and therefore not contain it. Equation (2), the functions phi and psi, pose conventions, and the claim that the resulting pose has no rotation about the up axis are also insufficiently specified and appear inconsistent with the sampled yaw rotations. These are central details rather than cosmetic omissions.

The proposed benchmarks are small—140 videos and 20 panoramas—and provide no uncertainty estimates, repeated stochastic generations, significance analysis, or human judgments. FID and especially FVD are unreliable at this sample size. Static frame grids also cannot establish temporal coherence or camera-motion accuracy.

Semantic fidelity is a significant unresolved tradeoff. The full model has the lowest CLIP score among dynamic baselines in Table 1, while Figure 6 shifts every method's CLIP curve by its own mean, concealing absolute differences. The claim that null-pitch conditioning maximizes content similarity is therefore not convincingly demonstrated, and cases where users intentionally request content associated with an extreme viewpoint are not tested.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript: essential definitions and trajectory-generation details are deferred to supplementary material, the inference-time use of the look-down caption as a negative prompt is ambiguous for novel prompts, and there is no clear commitment to release code, model weights, training annotations, or the processed training data. Dataset licensing and the implications of using filtered YouTube panoramic videos are also not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant limitation of text-to-video models: precise camera control under extreme pitch and roll. The gravity-aligned coordinate system makes the controls substantially more interpretable than first-frame-relative camera representations.

The central data pipeline is technically sensible and creative. Calibrated 360-degree videos permit perspective crops across the full viewing sphere, providing training orientations that are rare in conventional human-captured video while retaining real temporal content and estimated translation.

Null-pitch conditioning is a useful contribution addressing a clearly explained failure mode: semantic cues in captions can override geometrically specified camera angles. The ablation is strong, with its removal increasing pitch error from 9.35 to 15.78 degrees and gravity error from 11.67 to 17.72 degrees.

The empirical camera-control gains are substantial. On SpatialVID-extreme, the method obtains the best pitch and gravity errors by clear margins and the best relative rotation error among dynamic video-generation methods. The qualitative backflip and extreme-view examples support the quantitative findings.

The two proposed evaluations target limitations poorly covered by standard forward-facing video benchmarks. In particular, the prompt-camera entanglement benchmark isolates an interesting and under-studied conflict between semantic fidelity and geometric control.

The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually effective. It positions the method against relevant camera-controlled generation, panorama generation, and pose-estimation literature, while candidly acknowledging restrictions on translation augmentation and remaining visual artifacts.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the work provides a coherent combination of representation, data construction, conditioning, and evaluation advances. Although gravity-aware control overlaps conceptually with concurrent UCPE, the panorama-based sampling pipeline and null-pitch strategy provide meaningful differentiation.
weaknesses: The evaluation benchmark is small: SpatialVID-extreme contains only 140 manually filtered videos. FID and especially FVD can be unstable at this scale, yet the paper reports neither uncertainty nor repeated-generation statistics. This weakens fine-grained visual-quality comparisons.

Several comparisons confound the proposed method with backbone capacity and generation paradigm: the method uses WAN-2.2 5B, whereas UCPE uses WAN-2.1 and AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B; GEN3C is a static-scene novel-view method. These baselines remain informative, but they do not cleanly isolate the benefit of the proposed conditioning and training data.

Absolute-orientation evaluation depends on Perspective Fields, which is also used to estimate pitch when constructing SpatialVID-extreme. The paper provides no validation against sensor-derived or manually calibrated ground truth, and estimator reliability may degrade precisely at the extreme viewpoints of interest.

The method's gains in orientation control come with measurable tradeoffs: it has the lowest CLIP score among dynamic methods, worse FID than all listed dynamic baselines, and FVD that is only roughly competitive. Figure 6 mean-centers each method's CLIP curve, which illustrates variation but obscures absolute semantic quality.

Translation control is not convincingly demonstrated. Training can only reuse translations from source panoramas, the method has the worst TransErr among the dynamic approaches in Table 1 (0.72), and no targeted qualitative or quantitative translation study supports the prominent translation-control claim.

Ablations are limited largely to null-pitch conditioning. The paper does not isolate the effects of gravity alignment, absolute versus relative Pluecker conditioning, spherical trajectory sampling, training-set size, or the look-down negative-prompt mechanism.

The claimed absolute control excludes absolute yaw, which remains unconstrained. This convention is explained in the method, but the title, abstract, and broader claims of absolute camera control could more precisely state that the absolute reference applies to gravity-dependent pitch and roll.

The Pluecker-ray description appears technically questionable: the stated direction computation adds camera translation before normalization, whereas a ray direction normally depends only on rotation and intrinsics. If this reflects implementation rather than a notation error, it would affect the conditioning geometry and should be corrected or clarified.

Important reproducibility details, including the complete definitions of the coordinate transformations and camera encoder, are deferred to the supplement. The main paper promises benchmark release upon publication but does not make an equally explicit code, processed-annotation, or model-checkpoint commitment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant limitation of camera-controlled video generation: absolute, gravity-referenced pitch and roll, particularly under extreme rotations. The panoramic-video pipeline is a sensible way to overcome the strong orientation bias of conventional video datasets. It generates broad spherical viewpoint coverage while retaining real scene dynamics and translations.

Null-pitch conditioning identifies a meaningful prompt-camera conflict and is supported by controlled ablations. On WAN-2.2 5B, it reduces PitchErr from 14.39 to 8.36 degrees and GravityErr from 16.36 to 10.54 degrees; removing absolute rotations also causes a large degradation in the UCPE setting.
The approach is demonstrated across two backbones and both UCPE and Plücker conditioning, supporting the claim that it is not tied to one architecture.

The proposed extreme-orientation and prompt-camera-entanglement evaluations target weaknesses poorly captured by standard forward-facing benchmarks. Qualitative examples also show capabilities, such as backflip-like trajectories, that competing systems visibly fail to reproduce.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, appropriately situated relative to AC3D, UCPE, PreciseCam, and GEN3C, and candidly acknowledges limitations in translation augmentation and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The camera-control improvements come with a substantial quality and semantic-alignment tradeoff that is understated. For WAN-2.2, null-pitch conditioning worsens FVD from 895.2 to 1014.4 and CLIP from 22.0 to 20.6; the WAN-2.1 Plücker model has FVD 1041.6 versus 776.3 for PreciseCam+WAN. Describing these results as broadly competitive or on par is not fully convincing without uncertainty estimates or a study of the control-quality Pareto frontier.

The evaluation risks estimator circularity: Perspective Fields supplies gravity estimates in the training-data pipeline, helps select and annotate SpatialVID-extreme, and is then used to score generated pitch and gravity. Results should be validated with independent calibration, human judgments, or synthetic scenes with exact poses.

The benchmarks are small—138 videos for SpatialVID-extreme and only 20 panoramas for the entanglement benchmark—and the paper reports no confidence intervals, repeated generations, or statistical tests. FID and especially FVD can be unstable and biased at such sample sizes.

Evidence for full roll control is incomplete. Roll is not reported directly, and GravityErr cannot reliably expose roll errors when viewing near the poles because gravity approaches the optical axis. Dedicated roll trajectories and an independent roll metric are needed to substantiate the extreme-roll claims.

The term “absolute camera control” overstates what is physically grounded. Pitch and roll are gravity-referenced, but yaw remains arbitrary, translations come from relative SfM with uncertain scale, and evaluation normalizes translation magnitude. The framing should explicitly say absolute orientation with respect to gravity rather than generally absolute pose.

Baseline comparisons are partly confounded by different backbones, model sizes, training strategies, and input modalities. The cleanest matched comparison is against UCPE on WAN-2.1, where the absolute-orientation gain is useful but more modest than the headline results. Comparable training budgets and matched-data baselines would strengthen attribution.

Null-pitch captions are derived from one forward-facing crop and therefore do not necessarily describe the full panoramic scene. The strategy may teach the model to disregard prompt concepts outside the requested view rather than truly disentangling language and pose; tests involving localized objects, compositional prompts, and prompt-following judged independently of camera angle are missing.

Important reproducibility details are deferred to supplementary material, including training schedules and trajectory construction details. The main paper also lacks compute cost, generation protocol, seed/sample counts, and analysis of errors in SfM and gravity pseudo-labels. Release is promised only upon publication, so the benchmarks and results are not presently reproducible.

The use of thousands of YouTube-derived panoramic videos deserves clearer discussion of licensing, consent, privacy, and redistribution constraints, particularly because new crops and VLM-generated captions are created from this material.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant limitation of camera-controlled video generation: reliable control at extreme pitch and roll angles. The gravity-aligned representation is intuitive and potentially useful for cinematic applications.

The use of 360-degree videos to synthesize diverse camera trajectories is a sensible way to reduce the strong forward-facing bias of conventional video datasets. The pipeline supports multiple camera encodings and backbones rather than depending on one architecture.

Null-pitch conditioning identifies a real prompt-camera conflict and is supported by targeted ablations. For WAN-2.2 5B, removing it increases PitchErr from 8.36 degrees to 14.39 degrees and GravityErr from 10.54 degrees to 16.36 degrees.

The paper introduces two relevant evaluation settings, includes several contemporary baselines, and presents clear figures and a candid limitations discussion. weaknesses: The central framing overstates what is absolute or physically grounded. Yaw remains unconstrained, translation inherits an arbitrary SfM coordinate system, and evaluation explicitly normalizes trajectory scale. Consequently, claims such as controlling a translation by eight meters are not supported by metric-scale training or evaluation; the demonstrated absolute control is principally gravity-referenced pitch and roll.

The camera-accuracy evidence relies heavily on learned estimators: Perspective Fields both supplies gravity-related annotations and evaluates PitchErr/GravityErr, while VGGT evaluates relative rotation. These estimators are not validated on the generated, distorted, and extreme-angle imagery studied here. Without calibrated synthetic ground truth, manual measurements, or estimator agreement tests, improvements could partly reflect estimator bias or artifacts.

The headline comparison is confounded by backbone size, camera encoder, and training regime. The strongest orientation result uses WAN-2.2 5B, whereas important baselines use 1.3B or 2B models. In the controlled WAN-2.1/UCPE comparison, the gains over UCPE are more modest, while content and perceptual metrics deteriorate. The paper does not isolate the benefit of panoramic trajectory augmentation against a comparably trained conventional-data baseline.

Camera adherence comes with substantial quality costs that are underemphasized. For example, the WAN-2.1 Plücker model has FVD 1041.6 versus 776.3 for PreciseCam+WAN, and the WAN-2.2 model worsens FVD from 895.2 without null-pitch conditioning to 1014.4 with it while also lowering CLIP. The reported FID of 116.0 is the worst non-grayed result in the table. Thus the evidence does not yet establish a favorable overall fidelity-control tradeoff.

SpatialVID-extreme contains only 138 videos, and its reference videos do not correspond to the randomly substituted evaluation rotations. FID/FVD computed on such a small, mismatched set are difficult to interpret. The prompt-entanglement benchmark is likewise only 20 panoramas and 380 correlated prompt-angle pairs, with no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance analysis.

Null-pitch captions are described as representing the full scene, but a forward-looking crop can omit content visible at other yaw or pitch angles. The entanglement benchmark adopts essentially the same forward-caption/extreme-view construction used by the method, making it particularly favorable to the proposed conditioning strategy. Broader prompts and independently designed tests are needed.

The most diagnostic ablations are missing: training without panorama-based trajectory resampling, sensitivity to gravity/SfM errors, dataset size and filtering effects, pole-biased sampling, and the look-down negative-prompt mechanism. Removing absolute rotations is largely an information-removal sanity check rather than evidence that the proposed annotation pipeline is optimal.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Essential architecture, optimization, loss, sampling, and benchmark-generation details are deferred to supplementary material; no compute cost or variance is reported. The training source is a filtered YouTube subset, but licensing, redistribution, annotation release, and failure biases from discarding 38% of videos are not sufficiently addressed. Overall, the idea has merit, but the unsupported metric-control claims and weaknesses in evaluation favor rejection in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant limitation of camera-controlled video generation: existing relative-pose representations cannot specify pitch and roll with respect to gravity. The gravity-aligned coordinate system gives the controls a clear physical interpretation and enables challenging shots such as top-down views, barrel rolls, and full rotations.

The panorama-based training pipeline is well motivated. Sampling perspective crops over the viewing sphere directly counteracts the strong upright, forward-facing bias of ordinary videos and can generate varied trajectories without collecting a new sensor-equipped dataset.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple but insightful response to prompt-camera entanglement. The matched ablations provide convincing evidence: removing it substantially increases pitch and gravity errors, including a 72% pitch-error increase for the WAN-2.2 variant.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this problem. The method is tested with Plücker and UCPE conditioning and several video backbones, with comparisons to AC3D, UCPE, and PreciseCam-based pipelines. On SpatialVID-extreme, it consistently improves absolute orientation accuracy; the matched UCPE comparison also improves relative rotation error from 18.38 to 12.12.

The new SpatialVID-extreme and PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmarks target failure modes that conventional forward-facing benchmarks miss. The latter is particularly useful because it explicitly tests conflicts between textual semantics and requested camera pitch.

The presentation is clear and visually effective, and the paper appropriately acknowledges limitations involving translation augmentation, training-data artifacts, and occasional generation distortions.
weaknesses: The strongest gains are in camera-orientation fidelity, while visual quality and semantic alignment sometimes decline. For example, the WAN-2.1 Plücker model has substantially worse FVD than PreciseCam+WAN (1041.6 versus 776.3), and several variants have lower CLIP scores. The paper would benefit from human evaluation of realism, prompt fidelity, and camera adherence to establish the practical balance among these objectives.

SpatialVID-extreme contains only 138 videos. FID and especially FVD can be unstable at this scale, yet no confidence intervals, repeated sampling, or significance analysis are reported. The paper also relies on Perspective Fields, VGGT, and ViPE-derived measurements without validating their accuracy on generated videos with extreme orientations and distortions.

The benchmark does not fully mirror the headline operating range: its roll examples are created by 2D warping within only -40 to 40 degrees, whereas the paper emphasizes arbitrary orientations and full rotations. A controlled evaluation using known rendered camera trajectories, including near-pole and full-roll cases, would more directly verify the claims.

Translation control is less convincing than rotation control. The method cannot synthesize new translation trajectories during augmentation, uses translations inherited from source videos, and does not improve TransErr consistently. Claims about general camera control should therefore be qualified as primarily absolute orientation control.

Some comparisons conflate the proposed training pipeline with backbone size and finetuning strategy. The matched UCPE experiment is helpful, but an equally controlled decomposition of panorama trajectory sampling, gravity alignment, null-pitch captions, and look-down negative prompting would better identify which components produce the gains.

Reproducibility depends heavily on supplementary details not present in the supplied manuscript, including training hyperparameters, trajectory construction for evaluation, filtering thresholds, and the full definitions of the coordinate transformations. The benchmarks are promised for release rather than currently available, and the cost of on-the-fly VLM captioning is not quantified.
